title: From Headline to Hiring Signal
hook: Teaching a 3B language model to score candidates like a recruiter, and to say when it isn't sure

slides.title: From Headline to Hiring Signal
slides.subtitle: A real client project, built with Apziva as an AI Resident
slides.narration: This one's a real client project! Divyesh taught a language model to score job candidates the way a recruiter does. Let me show you how.

slides.title: The problem
bullets: A talent sourcing firm finds people for technology companies
Recruiters search with keywords that change for every role, then review every profile by hand
The best fit is often not at the top of the list; it might be the 7th
The goal: understand candidates, score their fit, rank them, and learn from reviewers
slides.narration: Recruiters were reviewing every profile by hand, and the best person was often buried halfway down the list. The firm wanted a system that understands and ranks candidates.

slides.title: Three stages, three skills

steps.label: Read
steps.detail: A few-shot LLM turns messy profile text into clean, structured JSON

steps.label: Judge
steps.detail: Qwen2.5-3B is fine-tuned with QLoRA to predict the reviewers' 0–100 screening score

steps.label: Know its limits
steps.detail: Retrieval over past candidates calibrates each score, explains it, and flags unsure cases

slides.narration: He built it in three stages: first the model learns to read profiles, then to judge them, and finally to know when it's out of its depth.

slides.title: Stage 1: Teaching the machine to read
bullets: Abbreviations normalised ("HR" → "human resources") so keyword search works
Told never to invent missing information
Batched 25 per call with per-row retry for malformed JSON
slides.narration: Every one of the 1,266 profiles came out as clean JSON with zero parsing errors, and job titles were normalised so the same role always has the same name.

slides.title: Stage 2: Teaching the machine to judge
bullets: QLoRA: the base model stays frozen in 4-bit; small LoRA adapters (rank 16) learn
A regression head predicts the score directly
Trained on MAE, the same metric it's evaluated on
Split stratified by job title, so every role is represented fairly
slides.narration: Fine-tuning a 3-billion-parameter model on free Kaggle GPUs? QLoRA made it possible by training less than one percent of the weights.

slides.title: Results on the untouched test set
slides.narration: The fine-tuned model cut the error by about 45 percent, and it ranks candidates in much the same order the reviewers did. That ranking is what matters most for a shortlist.

slides.title: What the model actually learned
slides.unit: How much the error grows when a field is shuffled
bullets: Reviewer scores are two-tiered: 20–40 or 80–100, with nobody between 40 and 60
Location turned out to be the strongest signal of all
slides.narration: He didn't stop at the score. Taking the model apart showed reviewers sorted people into strong and weak, and that location mattered more than anything else. That's worth auditing.

slides.title: Stage 3: Knowing what it doesn't know
bullets: Finds the 5 most similar past candidates and blends their scores with the model's
Embeddings come from the fine-tuned model itself, in the same forward pass
Built twice to compare: FAISS (speed) and ChromaDB (metadata filters)
Every score comes with evidence a recruiter can check
slides.narration: Retrieval here isn't about writing text. It calibrates the score, shows the recruiter similar past candidates as evidence, and flags the cases a human should look at closely.

slides.title: Responsible use
bullets: Decision support, never automatic rejection: every candidate is still reviewed by a person
Location can act as a proxy for things that must not influence hiring, so it's the first thing to audit
Small, imbalanced data: 260 titles, most with only a handful of examples
The client's candidate data is private and not in the repository
slides.narration: He's upfront about the limits: it's a helper for reviewers, not a decision maker, and the location finding needs auditing before any real-world use.

slides.title: What's next, and try it yourself
bullets: Next: when a reviewer stars the ideal candidate, re-rank the list around that choice
Biggest lesson: look at the label distribution before choosing a loss
The trained adapter is public on Hugging Face; all notebooks are on GitHub
slides.narration: Next up is the starring feature, so every review makes the list smarter. The model and notebooks are public, so you can try it yourself!
